# Pasta e Ceci

## Ingredients

- 250 g dried chickpeas, soaked overnight
- 1 rosemary sprig
- 200 g ditalini
- 3 cloves of garlic, sliced
- 4 tablespoons of olive oil
- 1 parmesan rind
- a handful of the cooked chickpeas, mashed
- salt and coarse black pepper

## Steps

1. Drain the soaked chickpeas, tip them into a heavy pot, and cover them with cold water by a good three fingers.
2. Add the rosemary sprig and the parmesan rind, bring the pot to a bare simmer, and cook for about an hour until the chickpeas crush easily against the side of the pot.
3. Warm the olive oil in a small pan and cook the garlic gently until it is pale gold, then pour the oil and garlic into the chickpea pot.
4. Scoop out a handful of the chickpeas and mash them against the side of the pot, then stir them back in to thicken the broth.
5. Add the ditalini straight to the chickpea pot and cook them in the broth, stirring often, until they are al dente.
6. Pull out the rosemary sprig and the parmesan rind, season with salt and pepper, and let the pot rest off the heat for ten minutes before serving.

## Notes

The pasta cooks in the chickpea pot, which is what makes the dish thick and comforting rather than thin and soupy. The mashed handful of chickpeas is doing real work, because that starch is what gives the broth its body before the ditalini break down at all. I never add tomato paste to this pot, and I think the rosemary and the parmesan rind give it plenty of depth without any. Soaking the dried chickpeas overnight is not optional if you want them creamy in an hour; unsoaked ones take two to three hours and even then stay a little firm in the middle. Keep the simmer low once the pasta goes in, because a rolling boil will break the ditalini apart and turn the pot cloudy. Add hot water if it tightens too much, since ditalini drink a surprising amount of broth. The dish thickens as it sits, so a second-day bowl is almost a different meal and wants a splash of water and a slow reheat. A final drizzle of raw olive oil in each bowl wakes the whole thing up. I break up a few of the whole chickpeas with the back of a spoon as I eat rather than mashing everything at the start, because I like the broth to stay a little varied rather than uniformly smooth. Dried chickpeas from a good shop are better than any tinned ones here, since the tinned sort are already soft and add almost no body to the pot. If you do use tinned chickpeas, cut the simmering time right down and add the pasta to a lighter broth. The rosemary sprig should be whole so you can pull it out cleanly at the end, and the parmesan rind does the same job as a stock cube but with far more depth. Cold weather and a bowl of this with a hunk of bread is about as good as a simple supper gets, and it costs almost nothing to make.
